Supervised machine learning: Basic framework, regression models and classification models. Linear regression, nonlinear regression, multiple regression, polynomial regression,lasso regression, ridge regression, stepwise regression, quantile regression, logistic regression.

## Supervised machine learning: Basic framework, regression models and classification models

Let's understand term machine learning. According to Dave Bergmann of IBM, Machine learning is a subset of AI where algorithms learn patterns from training data to make inferences about new data without explicit instructions. This pattern recognition ability enables machine learning models to make decisions or predictions without explicit, hard-coded instructions.

![](ml.jfif)

Though “machine learning” and “artificial intelligence” are often used interchangeably, they are not quite synonymous. In short: all machine learning is AI, but not all AI is machine learning.

Machine learning works through mathematical logic. The relevant characteristics (or "features") of each data point must therefore be expressed numerically, so that the data itself can be fed into a mathematical algorithm that will "learn" to map a given input to the desired output. The (often manual) process of choosing which aspects of data to use in machine learning algorithms is called feature selection. Feature extraction techniques refine data down to only its most relevant, meaningful dimensions.

## Types of machine learning

All machine learning methods can be categorized as one of three distinct learning paradigms: supervised learning, unsupervised learning or reinforcement learning, based on the nature of their training objectives and (often but not always) by the type of training data they entail.

Supervised learning trains a model to predict the “correct” output for a given input. It applies to tasks that require some degree of accuracy relative to some external “ground truth,” such as classification or regression. Unsupervised learning trains a model to discern intrinsic patterns, dependencies and correlations in data. Unlike in supervised learning, unsupervised learning tasks don’t involve any external ground truth against which its outputs should be compared.

Reinforcement learning (RL) trains a model to evaluate its environment and take an action that will garner the greatest reward. RL scenarios don’t entail the existence of a singular ground truth, but they do entail the existence of “good” and “bad” (or neutral) actions.

### Supervised learning

Supervised learning algorithms train models for tasks requiring accuracy, such as classification or regression. Supervised machine learning powers both state-of-the-art deep learning models and a wide array of traditional ML models still widely employed across industries.

*Regression models* predict continuous values, such as price, duration, temperature or size. Examples of traditional regression algorithms include linear regression, polynomial regression and state space models.

*Classification models* predict discrete values, such as the category (or class) a data point belongs to, a binary decision or a specific action to be taken. Examples of traditional classification algorithms include support vector machines (SVMs), Naïve Bayes and logistic regression.

Many supervised ML algorithms can be used for either task. For instance, the output of what’s nominally a regression algorithm can subsequently be used to inform a classification prediction.

## Machine Learning Case Study

### Build a Baseline Model

![](sea.webp)

Credit: https://share.google/VZsjc4wcgbifTAUZd

![](food.webp)

Credit: https://share.google/GJPqwS4zBoWp9Ej25

A Japanese company - selling packed sea urchin based food preps. Recently Japanese Food Regulation Authority made sea urchin based food manufacturing more stringent and adherence to nutritional consistency more stringent. 

Till now, company was receiving sea urchin supplies from local fishermen. Company washes, preserves and packages the sea urchins and sends in the market. In this process, the sea urchin's nutritional values were not managed by company as they just collect and market them. Due to difference in quality, there were various voices raised by the food experts so that people get consistent quality.

Company management decides to introduce a 30 day feed plan for the supplies of the sea urchins before they are packed and sent to the market. So, they wanted an real world evidence of a diet plan that can make sea urchins width equal and consistent. The company wants to calibrate width and initial volume vs. the food regime. The data collected is shown below:

```{r}

library(tidymodels)
library(readr)

urchins <-

  read_csv("https://tidymodels.org/start/models/urchins.csv") |>
  
    setNames(c("food_regime", "initial_volume", "width")) |> 

    mutate(food_regime = factor(food_regime, levels = c("Initial", "Low", "High")))

head(urchins)

```

To keep the diet regime composition secret, company codifies the three levels of diets as Initial, Low and High. Number of observations in the data is `r nrow(urchins)`.

Let's plot the data:

```{r}

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(urchins,
       
       aes(x=initial_volume, y=width, colour = food_regime)) +
  
      geom_point() +
  
      geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) +
  
      labs(title="Sea Urchin: Width Vs initial volume",
           y = "Width",
           x = "initial volume",
           subtitle = "Based on sample of 72 urchins",
           caption = "Study conducted by IABM Students MBA Part 2") +
  
  theme_classic()

```


If we observe the plot, we can see that food regime has different effect for the width vs initial volume relationship. This gives us an indication that food regime interacts with width and initial volume relationship. This a significant information for building a machine learning model. Since the slopes appear to be different for at least two of the feeding regimes, let’s build a model that allows for two-way interactions. Specifying an R formula with our variables in this way:

`width ~ initial_volume * food_regime`

We can also check the distribution of width and initial volume acorss the sample:

```{r}

hist(urchins$width, main="Distribution of width : Sea Urchin", n=30)

hist(urchins$initial_volume, main="Distribution of initial volume : Sea Urchin", n=30)

```

We can see that the distribution of the width and initial volume of sea urchin sample is near to normal bell shaped curve. We can check normality of a variable through statistical tests also:

```{r}

# applying shapiro-Wilk test

shapiro.test(urchins$width)

shapiro.test(urchins$initial_volume)

```

To check the assumption of normality, Shapiro-Wilk tests were conducted on the sample of 72 urchins. The results indicated that the distribution of initial volume (W = 0.91, p < .001) and width (W = 0.96, p = .016) both significantly deviated from normality.

Let's also check for missing values in the data:

```{r}

sum(is.na(urchins))

```

So, there is no missing values in the dataset. 

The width and initial_volume both are numerical variables and we want to predict width based on initial_volume subject to food_regime. This can be modeled with linear regression model. Following command chunck shows this:

```{r}

lm_mod = linear_reg()

lm_fit = lm_mod |>
  
  fit(width ~ initial_volume * food_regime, data = urchins)

lm_fit

```


Let's see the model in better (tidy) format:

```{r}

tidy(lm_fit)

```

With `dotwhisker` package, we can also observe model visually:

```{r}

library(dotwhisker)

tidy(lm_fit) |>
  dwplot(dot_args = list(size = 2, color = "#7C7C7C"),
         whisker_args = list(color = "#7C7C7C"),
         vline = geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50", linetype = 2))


```


Now let's create new set of observations to predict the width of sea urchin using the regression model we buold just now.

```{r}

new_obs = expand.grid(initial_volume = 20, 
                       food_regime = c("Initial","Low","High"))

```


Let's predict:

```{r}

mean_pred = predict(lm_fit, new_data = new_obs)

mean_pred

```


Or we can also predict with confidence interval:

```{r}

conf_int_pred = predict(lm_fit, new_data = new_obs,
        type = "conf_int")

conf_int_pred

```

Let's combine both predictions and visualise:

```{r}

plot_data <- 
  new_obs |> 
  bind_cols(mean_pred) |> 
  bind_cols(conf_int_pred)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = food_regime)) + 
  geom_point(aes(y = .pred)) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = .pred_lower, 
                    ymax = .pred_upper),
                width = .2) + 
  labs(y = "urchin size")

```

Another way of building model is using Bayesian approach. In Bayesian approach, the prior distribution is used to build model. Here we need to first declare prior probabilities first and then, we do model building using different engine. 

```{r}

# set the prior distribution
prior_dist <- rstanarm::student_t(df = 1)   # Setting up prior probability using t distribution

set.seed(123)

# make the parsnip model
bayes_mod <-   
  linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("stan",                          # Engine for Bayesian model
             prior_intercept = prior_dist,
             prior = prior_dist,
             refresh = 0)

# train the model
bayes_fit <- 
  bayes_mod |> 
  fit(width ~ initial_volume * food_regime, data = urchins)

print(bayes_fit, digits = 5)

```

Let's visualize the Bayesian model:

```{r}

bayes_plot_data <- 
  new_obs |> 
  bind_cols(predict(bayes_fit, new_data = new_obs)) |> 
  bind_cols(predict(bayes_fit, new_data = new_obs, type = "conf_int"))

ggplot(bayes_plot_data, aes(x = food_regime)) + 
  geom_point(aes(y = .pred)) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = .pred_lower, ymax = .pred_upper), width = .2) + 
  labs(y = "urchin size") + 
  ggtitle("Bayesian model with t(1) prior distribution")

```


## Data Pre-Processing

Data pre-processing is necessary before building model. In Sea urchin case study we have a perfect data set hence we could straight away jump to model building however it is not the case everytime. You will get messy data most of the time. You need to process the messy data into a polished and organized before building any model. Package `recipes` is the R package we will use to process the data. So, let's begin.

The package `Recipes` has inbuilt series of preprocessing steps, such as:

* Converting qualitative predictors to indicator variables (also known as dummy variables),

* Transforming data to be on a different scale (e.g., taking the logarithm of a variable),

* Transforming whole groups of predictors together,

* Extracting key features from raw variables (e.g., getting the day of the week out of a date variable),

To use code, you will need to install (use `install.packages("packagename")` command) the following packages: `mlbench, themis,here, kableExtra, lubridate, nycflights13, skimr, tidymodels`, and `timeDate`.

```{r}

library(tidymodels)      # for the recipes package, along with the rest of tidymodels

# Helper packages
library(skimr) 
library(mlbench)
library(themis)
library(stringr)

```


Soybean is the crop majorly grown in Western India and the crop is prone to 16 different types of diseases. We use following dataset to build a classification model to identify the class of disease:

```{r}

data("Soybean", package = "mlbench")

soy = as_tibble(Soybean)

glimpse(soy)

```

In the dataset, we have 683 rows and 36 variables. Let's look at the missingness in the data:

```{r}

## Quick look at missingness and class balance
colSums(is.na(soy)) |> 
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> 
  head(10)

```

Let's also check class imbalance in the `Class` variable that is decision variable (`y`): 

```{r}

soy |> 
  count(Class, sort = TRUE) |> 
  print(n = 20)

```

We can clearly see class imbalance here. The disease class `herbicide-injury` has only 8 observations and disease class `brown-spot` has 92 observations. When we build model on such imbalanced data, the model will get more discriminant features from higher frequency class and very less discriminant features from the low freqquency class. Consequenly, model will be biased towards higher frequency class which will create a model that can not be reliable. 

To sort out this, we need to balance the class frequencies to the equal proportions in the data. But, first we build a classification model with all data preprocessing needed:

### Data Split

We train the model on 80% of the data and keep 20% data to test the model. The data is split through stratified random sampling:

```{r}

set.seed(42)
split      <- initial_split(soy, prop = 0.8, strata = Class)
soy_train  <- training(split)
soy_test   <- testing(split)
 
soy_train

soy_test

```

You can see that out of `r nrow(soy)` observations, soy_train dataset contains 80% observations i.e. `r nrow(soy_train)` observations and soy_test dataset contains 20% observations i.e. `r nrow(soy_test)` observations. 

### Build the preprocessing `recipe`

This is the core of the exercise: every cleaning/encoding
Decision is captured as a *recipe step*, learned only on the training set, then reproducibly applied to any new data.
 
```{r} 
 
soy_recipe <-
  recipe(Class ~ ., data = soy_train) |>
 
  # (a) Drop predictors that are (near) constant -> add no signal
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) |>
 
  # (b) Handle missing values in categorical predictors
  #     Bagged trees impute using the other predictors' patterns,
  #     which works well for structured agronomic survey data.
  step_impute_bag(all_nominal_predictors(), impute_with = imp_vars(all_predictors())) |>
 
  # (c) Collapse rarely-occurring factor levels into "other"
  #     (prevents unstable dummy columns from very rare categories)
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.03, other = "other_level") |>
 
  # (d) Ensure factor levels seen in test/new data don't break the model
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
 
  # (e) One-hot / dummy encode categorical predictors for models
  #     that need numeric input
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE) |>
 
  # (f) Remove any dummy columns that are (still) near-zero variance
  #     after encoding
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) |>
 
  # (g) Remove highly correlated dummy columns (redundant info)
  step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.9) |>
 
  # (h) Scale numeric predictors (harmless here, essential if you
  #     later add real-valued agronomic measurements e.g. rainfall_mm)
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
 
  # (i) Address class imbalance (19 disease classes, some very rare)
  #     using up-sampling on the TRAINING data only
  step_upsample(Class, over_ratio = 0.5)
 
```


### Inspect the recipe without training a model

`prep()` estimates all step parameters (imputation models, which
levels to pool, correlation matrix, normalization mean/sd, etc.) using soy_train ONLY - no leakage from soy_test.
 
```{r}

soy_prep <- prep(soy_recipe, training = soy_train)
soy_prep

```
 
### Data Pransformation for Model 
 
`bake()` applies the learned transformations to produce the final model-ready data frame:

```{r}

train_baked <- bake(soy_prep, new_data = NULL)   # transformed training data
test_baked  <- bake(soy_prep, new_data = soy_test)  # test data, same transforms
 
dim(train_baked)
dim(test_baked)
sum(is.na(train_baked))   # should be 0 - imputation worked

```
 
### Plug the recipe into a modeling workflow

We use random forest algorithm to build the model. 

```{r}

rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")
 
soy_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(soy_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_spec)
 
soy_fit <- fit(soy_workflow, data = soy_train)
 
```


### Evaluate on held-out test data

In the previous step, we have built a machine learning model named as `soy_fit` and to test the accuracy of the model, we use test data and create prediction of the diseases based on the predictors:

```{r}

soy_preds <- predict(soy_fit, new_data = soy_test) |>
  bind_cols(soy_test |> select(Class))
 
accuracy(soy_preds, truth = Class, estimate = .pred_class)

```

We can see that the accuracy of the model is 92.8% which means out of 100 attempts of classification, model is able to predict accurately is 92.8%. 

Let's deep dive into classification accuracy using confusion matrix:

```{r}

soy_preds |> conf_mat(truth = Class, estimate = .pred_class) |>
  summary() |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("accuracy", "kap"))
 
```

Let's evaluate model accuracy for each class of disease in soybean:

```{r}

soy_probs <- predict(soy_fit, new_data = soy_test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(soy_test |> select(Class))
 
soy_probs |> head()
## Columns look like: .pred_brown-spot, .pred_frog-eye-leaf-spot, ... , Class

```

### Multiclass ROC (one-vs-rest)

The `roc_curve()` automatically does one-vs-rest for a multi-level truth column when you pass all the .pred_* probability columns.

```{r} 
 
prob_cols <- names(soy_probs) |> str_subset("^\\.pred_")
 
roc_data <- roc_curve(
  soy_probs,
  truth = Class,
  !!!syms(prob_cols)
)
 
## Per-class AUC (one-vs-rest)
## a multiclass setting we loop over each class, re-code it as a
## binary "this class vs. all others" problem, and score that.
class_levels <- levels(soy_probs$Class)
 
roc_auc_by_class <- map_dfr(class_levels, function(cls) {
  prob_col <- paste0(".pred_", cls)
 
  binary_truth <- factor(
    if_else(soy_probs$Class == cls, cls, "other"),
    levels = c(cls, "other")   # cls = "event" / first level
  )
 
  bin_auc <- roc_auc(
    tibble(truth = binary_truth, prob = soy_probs[[prob_col]]),
    truth = truth,
    prob,
    event_level = "first"
  )
 
  tibble(.level = cls, .estimate = bin_auc$.estimate)
})
 
print(roc_auc_by_class, n = Inf)
 
## Overall macro-average AUC (what you'd usually report as "the" AUC)
roc_auc_macro <- roc_auc(
  soy_probs,
  truth = Class,
  !!!syms(prob_cols)
)
print(roc_auc_macro)
 
## ---- 6a. Quick built-in plot: one ROC curve per class, faceted ----
autoplot(roc_data) +
  labs(title = "One-vs-Rest ROC Curves per Soybean Disease Class")
 
## ---- 6b. All classes overlaid on ONE plot, AUC in the legend ------
auc_labels <- roc_auc_by_class |>
  mutate(label = paste0(.level, " (AUC = ", round(.estimate, 2), ")"))
 
roc_data |>
  left_join(auc_labels, by = ".level") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity, color = label)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_abline(lty = 3, color = "grey50") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title    = "Multiclass ROC Curves — Soybean Disease Classification",
    subtitle = "One-vs-rest, colored by disease class",
    x = "1 - Specificity (False Positive Rate)",
    y = "Sensitivity (True Positive Rate)",
    color = "Disease (AUC)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 8))

```

Let's discuss each part of Multi-Class ROC curves:

- $$ Sensitivity (True Positive Rate) = True_Positive_Cases / (True_Positive_Cases + False_Negative_Cases) $$

- $$ Specificity (False Positive Rate) = True_Negative_Cases / (True_Negative_Cases + False_Positive_Cases) $$


### Concluding Remarks

This analysis demonstrated an end-to-end multiclass classification pipeline for diagnosing soybean diseases from categorical agronomic and environmental observations. The `recipes` package handled the preprocessing burden reproducibly and without data leakage — filtering near-zero-variance predictors, imputing missing symptom records via bagged trees, pooling rare factor levels, one-hot encoding, removing redundant correlated features, and upsampling rare disease classes — all learned strictly on the training split and applied identically to the held-out test data.

The random forest classifier trained on this preprocessed data was evaluated using one-vs-rest ROC curves for each disease class rather than a single aggregate accuracy figure, since accuracy alone can mask poor performance on rarer or harder-to-distinguish diseases. Per-class AUC values reveal which diseases the model separates cleanly from all others (curves hugging the top-left corner, AUC near 1.0) versus which ones it confuses with visually or symptomatically similar conditions (curves closer to the diagonal, AUC near 0.5). This class-by-class view is more actionable for an agribusiness context than a single overall score — it tells you specifically which diseases a field-deployed diagnostic tool can be trusted on, and which would still need expert/agronomist confirmation before acting on the model's flag.

**Practical takeaway:** the preprocessing recipe is reusable well beyond this dataset — swap in real farm records (soil tests, weather logs, crop-cam imagery-derived features, past yield data) and the same `step_impute_*` → `step_other`/`step_novel` → `step_dummy` → `step_corr`/`step_nzv` → `step_normalize` → `step_upsample` sequence provides a robust, leakage-free foundation for any agribusiness classification problem — whether that's disease diagnosis, loan-default risk for agri-lending, or yield-grade prediction.


---

## Regression Methods

Regression methods are used to build model to predict the estimate or classify an obervation. In this section we will cover linear regression, nonlinear regression, multiple regression, polynomial regression,lasso regression, ridge regression, stepwise regression, quantile regression and logistic regression.

All examples use ONE simulated crop-yield dataset so you can compare techniques on the same problem:

**Predict crop YIELD (kg/hectare) from rainfall, fertilizer,temperature, and soil pH — plus a binary GOOD_YIELD outcome**

So, let's begin with calling the libraries required:

```{r}

# install.packages(c("glmnet", "quantreg", "ggplot2"))
library(glmnet)     # ridge & lasso
library(quantreg)   # quantile regression
library(ggplot2)    # plotting

```

### Simulate Data

We create a dataset of 200 observations and variables are as follows:

- `rainfall_mm`: Average rainfall measured in mm using mean 800 and standard deviation 150. 
- `fertilizer_kg`: Fertilizer consumed in KG using max use 150 Kg and min use 20 Kg. 
- `temperature_C`: Temperature measured in degree centigrade with mean 27 and standard deviation 3.
- `soil_ph`: Soil PH created with mean 6.5 and standard deviation 0.5. 
- `yeild_kg_ha`: Yeild per Hectare using a regression equation. 

We create a dataset by combining all the variables and we also add one more factor variable - `good_yield` using `if_else` logic. 

```{r}

set.seed(123)
n <- 200

rainfall_mm  <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 800, sd = 150), 1)
fertilizer_kg<- round(runif(n, 20, 150), 1)
temperature_C<- round(rnorm(n, mean = 27, sd = 3), 1)
soil_ph      <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 6.5, sd = 0.5), 2)

## Yield has a linear-ish relationship with rainfall/fertilizer/pH,
## but a NONLINEAR (diminishing-returns) relationship with fertilizer,
## and a curved (polynomial) relationship with temperature (yield
## drops off if it gets too hot or too cold - not just "more is better")

yield_kg_ha <- 2000 +
  2.5   * rainfall_mm +
  40    * sqrt(fertilizer_kg) -             # diminishing returns
  15    * (temperature_C - 27)^2 +          # optimal temp ~27C
  300   * soil_ph +
  rnorm(n, 0, 200)

crop <- data.frame(rainfall_mm, fertilizer_kg, temperature_C, soil_ph, yield_kg_ha)

## Binary outcome for logistic regression: "good yield" = above median
crop$good_yield <- factor(ifelse(crop$yield_kg_ha > median(crop$yield_kg_ha), 1, 0))


glimpse(crop)

```


### Train/test split (80/20)

```{r}

set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = 0.8 * n)
train <- crop[train_idx, ]
test  <- crop[-train_idx, ]

```

### LINEAR REGRESSION

To understand linear regression, we build mode with One predictor, straight-line relationship: yield vs. rainfall

```{r}

lm_simple <- lm(yield_kg_ha ~ rainfall_mm, data = train)
summary(lm_simple)

```

A simple linear regression was conducted to examine whether rainfall predicted crop yield. The overall model was statistically significant, *F*(1, 158) = 158.10, *p* < .001, and explained approximately 50% of the variance in yield, *R*² = .50, adjusted *R*² = .497.

Rainfall was a significant positive predictor of yield, *b* = 2.37, *SE* = 0.19, *t*(158) = 12.57, *p* < .001. For every additional millimeter of rainfall, yield increased by approximately 2.37 kg/hectare, holding all else constant. The intercept, *b* = 4299.77, *SE* = 151.51, *t*(158) = 28.38, *p* < .001, represents the model's predicted yield when rainfall is zero, though this value has limited practical interpretation since zero rainfall falls well outside the observed range of the data.

Let's check the relationship using visualization:

```{r}

ggplot(train, aes(rainfall_mm, yield_kg_ha)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Linear Regression: Yield vs. Rainfall")

```

### MULTIPLE REGRESSION

Now, we build model with Several predictors, each assumed to have a straight-line (additive) effect on yield:

```{r}

lm_multiple <- lm(yield_kg_ha ~ rainfall_mm + fertilizer_kg + temperature_C + soil_ph,
                   data = train)
summary(lm_multiple)
## Compare R-squared to the simple model - more predictors usually

```

Two regression models were compared to evaluate the predictors of crop yield. The simple linear regression, using rainfall alone, was statistically significant and explained approximately 50% of the variance in yield, *R*² = .50, adjusted *R*² = .497, *F*(1, 158) = 158.10, *p* < .001. Adding three additional predictors — fertilizer application, temperature, and soil pH — produced a multiple regression model that was also statistically significant, *F*(4, 155) = 70.30, *p* < .001, and explained a larger proportion of variance in yield, *R*² = .64, adjusted *R*² = .636.

The increase in adjusted *R*² from .497 to .636 indicates that the additional predictors accounted for meaningful variance in yield beyond rainfall alone, rather than merely adding noise (adjusted *R*², unlike *R*², penalizes the inclusion of uninformative predictors, making it the more appropriate statistic for comparing models of different sizes). This is further supported by the reduction in residual standard error from 333.1 to 283.5 kg/hectare, reflecting improved prediction accuracy.

Examining individual predictors in the multiple regression model, rainfall remained a strong, statistically significant positive predictor of yield, *b* = 2.34, *SE* = 0.16, *t*(155) = 14.46, *p* < .001, with a coefficient nearly identical to its estimate in the simple regression (*b* = 2.37), suggesting its effect on yield is robust to the inclusion of other variables. Fertilizer application was also a significant positive predictor, *b* = 2.53, *SE* = 0.60, *t*(155) = 4.25, *p* < .001, as was soil pH, *b* = 278.49, *SE* = 44.70, *t*(155) = 6.23, *p* < .001, which showed the largest standardized influence relative to its measurement scale. Temperature, however, was not a statistically significant predictor in this model, *b* = −0.64, *SE* = 7.70, *t*(155) = −0.08, *p* = .934.

Let's predict check the RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error):

```{r}

pred_multi <- predict(lm_multiple, newdata = test)
sqrt(mean((pred_multi - test$yield_kg_ha)^2))   # test RMSE

```

The test RMSE of 372.64 kg/hectare represents the typical magnitude of error when the multiple regression model predicts crop yield on **data it has not seen before** (the held-out test set). In other words, on average, the model's yield predictions deviate from actual yield by roughly 372.64 kg/hectare.

- The training-set residual standard error was 283.5 kg/hectare — noticeably lower than the test RMSE of 372.64.
- This gap (283.5 vs. 372.64) is a signal worth flagging: the model fits the training data better than it generalizes to new data. Some of this is expected (models almost always perform somewhat worse on unseen data), but a gap this size also lines up with what you found in the coefficient output — temperature was included as a plain linear term even though its true relationship with yield is quadratic (peaking at an optimal temperature). Because the model can't capture that curvature, it likely makes systematically larger errors on test observations with temperatures far from the training set's typical range, inflating the test RMSE.

- To assess whether 372.64 kg/hectare is "good" or "bad," it should be compared against the scale of the outcome itself — e.g., as a percentage of mean yield (mean(train$yield_kg_ha) would give you that denominator). A RMSE that's small relative to typical yield (say, under 10%) suggests reasonably useful predictions for advisory purposes; one that's large relative to typical yield suggests the model isn't precise enough to act on without caution.

- This is exactly the kind of gap the **polynomial regression** step (correctly modeling temperature's curvature) should help close — comparing this multiple-regression test RMSE against the polynomial model's test RMSE would be a natural next check, and a good addition to your assignment's Part C if you want students to explicitly connect "which model generalizes best" rather than just "which model fits training data best."

### POLYNOMIAL REGRESSION

We build polynomial model that Captures a curved relationship - here, yield peaks at an  OPTIMAL temperature rather than rising or falling monotonically.

```{r}

lm_poly <- lm(yield_kg_ha ~ poly(temperature_C, 2) + rainfall_mm + fertilizer_kg + soil_ph,
              data = train)
summary(lm_poly)

ggplot(train, aes(temperature_C, yield_kg_ha)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), color = "darkorange") +
  labs(title = "Polynomial Regression: Yield vs. Temperature (degree 2)")

```

A polynomial regression model was estimated to test whether allowing temperature a curved (quadratic) relationship with yield would improve on the purely linear multiple regression model. The polynomial model was statistically significant, *F*(5, 154) = 130.50, *p* < .001, and explained substantially more variance in yield than the linear multiple regression model, *R*² = .809, adjusted *R*² = .803, compared to *R*² = .645, adjusted *R*² = .636 previously.

The quadratic term for temperature was highly significant, *b* = −2412.82, *SE* = 209.60, *t*(154) = −11.51, *p* < .001, while the linear temperature term was not, *b* = 11.13, *SE* = 211.05, *t*(154) = 0.05, *p* = .958. This pattern confirms what the earlier linear model's non-significant temperature coefficient had obscured: temperature does meaningfully affect yield, but through a **curved, not straight-line, relationship** — consistent with an agronomic optimum temperature, where yield is highest at a moderate temperature and declines when conditions are either too cool or too hot. The negative sign on the squared term indicates an inverted-U (concave-down) curve, as expected.

Rainfall, *b* = 2.47, *SE* = 0.12, *t*(154) = 20.64, *p* < .001, fertilizer, *b* = 2.57, *SE* = 0.44, *t*(154) = 5.87, *p* < .001, and soil pH, *b* = 291.51, *SE* = 32.89, *t*(154) = 8.86, *p* < .001, all remained significant positive predictors, with coefficient estimates very similar to the linear multiple regression model — indicating their linear effects on yield were already well-captured and are not confounded with temperature's curvature.

The residual standard error also dropped notably, from 283.5 kg/hectare (linear multiple regression) to 208.6 kg/hectare (polynomial), reflecting a considerably tighter fit to the training data once temperature's true functional form was correctly specified.

**Practical takeaway:** This is a clean illustration of a common modeling mistake — a predictor can appear "non-significant" in a linear model not because it doesn't matter, but because the model was given the wrong functional form to detect it. Once quadratic curvature was allowed, temperature emerged as one of the most important predictors in the model (via its squared term).

One useful next step for your assignment: compute this model's **test RMSE** (the same way as before, using `predict(lm_poly, newdata = test)`) and compare it directly against the 372.64 kg/hectare from the linear multiple regression — that comparison will tell students concretely whether correctly modeling temperature's curvature also improves *generalization*, not just training fit.

```{r}

preds_poly = predict(lm_poly, newdata = test)

sqrt(mean((preds_poly - test$yield_kg_ha)^2))   # test RMSE

```

We can see that RMSE is now reduced to 203.59 from 372.64. There is an improvement in accuracy of the model. 


### NONLINEAR REGRESSION (nls)

Now, we fit a nonlinear functional FORM (not just apolynomial in the linear-model framework)here a Michaelis-Menten style diminishing-returns curve for fertilizer using   yield = Vmax * fertilizer / (K + fertilizer).

```{r}

nls_fert <- nls(
  yield_kg_ha ~ Vmax * fertilizer_kg / (K + fertilizer_kg),
  data  = train,
  start = list(Vmax = 6000, K = 50)   # starting guesses required for nls
)
summary(nls_fert)

ggplot(train, aes(fertilizer_kg, yield_kg_ha)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict(nls_fert)), color = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Nonlinear Regression: Diminishing Returns on Fertilizer")

```

### STEPWISE REGRESSION

When we build model we use a set of predictors. All predictors do not contribute to the model and still create noise and increases variance. Here, we use STEPWISE REGRESSION which automatically selects a subset of predictors by adding/removing predictors to optimize AIC (lower = better trade-off of fit vs. complexity). 

```{r}

full_model <- lm(yield_kg_ha ~ rainfall_mm + fertilizer_kg + temperature_C + soil_ph,
                  data = train)
null_model <- lm(yield_kg_ha ~ 1, data = train)

step_model <- stats::step(
  null_model,
  scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
  direction = "both",   # "forward", "backward", or "both"
  trace = FALSE
)
summary(step_model)
formula(step_model)   # which predictors survived

```

A stepwise regression procedure (bidirectional selection based on AIC) was conducted to identify the subset of predictors that best explained crop yield, starting from an intercept-only model and considering rainfall, fertilizer, temperature, and soil pH as candidate predictors. The procedure selected a final model retaining rainfall, soil pH, and fertilizer, while **removing temperature entirely** from the model.

The selected model was statistically significant, *F*(3, 156) = 94.33, *p* < .001, and explained approximately 64.5% of the variance in yield, *R*² = .645, adjusted *R*² = .638. Rainfall was the strongest predictor, *b* = 2.34, *SE* = 0.16, *t*(156) = 14.64, *p* < .001, followed by soil pH, *b* = 278.74, *SE* = 44.45, *t*(156) = 6.27, *p* < .001, and fertilizer, *b* = 2.53, *SE* = 0.59, *t*(156) = 4.27, *p* < .001. All three retained predictors were significant positive predictors of yield.

**Comparison to the full linear multiple regression model:**

| Model | Predictors | Adjusted R² | Residual SE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full linear multiple | rainfall + fertilizer + temperature + soil pH | .636 | 283.5 |
| Stepwise-selected | rainfall + fertilizer + soil pH | .638 | 282.6 |

Notably, the stepwise model achieves a *marginally higher* adjusted R² (.638 vs. .636) and lower residual standard error (282.6 vs. 283.5) than the full model — **despite dropping a predictor**. This is expected: adjusted R² penalizes unnecessary predictors, and since temperature's *linear* term was non-significant in the full model (*p* = .934, from your earlier output), removing it slightly improves the fit efficiency without sacrificing explanatory power.

**Important caveat worth flagging (especially for a student assignment):** this result illustrates a key limitation of stepwise selection rather than a genuine insight about temperature's importance. Temperature was correctly dropped *as a linear term*, but your polynomial regression model showed temperature's quadratic term was highly significant (*p* < .001) and substantially improved fit (adjusted R² = .803). Stepwise selection using `step()` only ever considered rainfall, fertilizer, temperature, and soil pH as **linear terms** — it never had the opportunity to discover the curved relationship, because `poly(temperature_C, 2)` was never in its candidate scope. This is a classic pitfall of stepwise/AIC-based selection: it can only select among the functional forms you explicitly offer it, and will confidently discard a genuinely important predictor if its true effect doesn't match the form tested.

**Practical takeaway:** stepwise regression is useful for pruning redundant linear predictors efficiently, but it is not a substitute for exploring nonlinear relationships first (via EDA plots or domain knowledge) — a variable dropped by stepwise selection may still be highly important if given the right functional form, as shown here.

### RIDGE REGRESSION

RIDGE REGRESSION Shrinks ALL coefficients toward zero (L2 penalty) - keeps every predictor but reduces overfitting/multicollinearity impact. Let's check how it works now: 

```{r}

x_train <- as.matrix(train[, c("rainfall_mm", "fertilizer_kg", "temperature_C", "soil_ph")])
y_train <- train$yield_kg_ha
x_test  <- as.matrix(test[,  c("rainfall_mm", "fertilizer_kg", "temperature_C", "soil_ph")])

ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0)   # alpha = 0 -> ridge
plot(ridge_cv)
best_lambda_ridge <- ridge_cv$lambda.min

ridge_model <- glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0, lambda = best_lambda_ridge)
coef(ridge_model)

```

Let's evaluate RIDGE MODEL:

```{r}

pred_ridge <- predict(ridge_model, newx = x_test)
sqrt(mean((pred_ridge - test$yield_kg_ha)^2))   # test RMSE

```

### LASSO REGRESSION

LASSO REGRESSION shrinks coefficients toward zero AND can set some exactly to zero (L1 penalty) - performs automatic variable selection.

```{r}

lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1)   # alpha = 1 -> lasso
plot(lasso_cv)
best_lambda_lasso <- lasso_cv$lambda.min

lasso_model <- glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1, lambda = best_lambda_lasso)
coef(lasso_model)   # predictors shrunk to exactly 0 are effectively dropped
pred_lasso <- predict(lasso_model, newx = x_test)
sqrt(mean((pred_lasso - test$yield_kg_ha)^2))   # test RMSE

```


### QUANTILE REGRESSION

Models a specific PERCENTILE of the outcome (not just the mean) - e.g. the 10th percentile is useful for "worst-case" yield planning, the 90th for best-case

```{r}
qr_median <- rq(yield_kg_ha ~ rainfall_mm + fertilizer_kg + temperature_C + soil_ph,
                 data = train, tau = 0.5)   # tau = 0.5 -> median regression
summary(qr_median)

qr_low  <- rq(yield_kg_ha ~ rainfall_mm + fertilizer_kg, data = train, tau = 0.10)
qr_high <- rq(yield_kg_ha ~ rainfall_mm + fertilizer_kg, data = train, tau = 0.90)

ggplot(train, aes(rainfall_mm, yield_kg_ha)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_quantile(quantiles = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), color = "purple") +
  labs(title = "Quantile Regression: 10th / 50th / 90th Percentile Yield")

```

### LOGISTIC REGRESSION

Now we want to classify the yield as Good For a BINARY outcome - here, whether yield is "good"(1) or "bad" (0). 

```{r}

log_model <- glm(good_yield ~ rainfall_mm + fertilizer_kg + temperature_C + soil_ph,
                  data = train, family = binomial)
summary(log_model)

## Predicted probabilities and classification on test data
pred_prob  <- predict(log_model, newdata = test, type = "response")
pred_class <- factor(ifelse(pred_prob > 0.5, 1, 0))
table(Predicted = pred_class, Actual = test$good_yield)   # confusion matrix
mean(pred_class == test$good_yield)                       # accuracy

```


## ============================================================
## SUMMARY — When to use which
## ============================================================
## Linear        - one predictor, straight-line relationship
## Multiple      - several predictors, each additive/linear
## Polynomial    - curved relationship still fit within lm() framework
## Nonlinear(nls)- true nonlinear functional form (e.g. saturation,
##                 growth curves) - you must specify the equation
## Stepwise      - automatic predictor selection via AIC
## Ridge         - many/correlated predictors, keep all, shrink coefficients
## Lasso         - many predictors, want automatic feature selection
## Quantile      - care about a specific percentile, not just the mean
##                 (e.g. worst-case/best-case yield planning)
## Logistic      - binary outcome (success/failure, good/bad, yes/no)
## ============================================================
